section.title: The First Journey: Cyprus and Pisidian Antioch
section.sectionRationale: The gospel now moves out on purpose. The Spirit sets apart Barnabas and Saul at Antioch, and the first missionary journey begins. On Cyprus a sorcerer is silenced and a proconsul believes; at Pisidian Antioch Paul preaches his first recorded sermon, tracing Israel's story to Jesus, the risen Savior in whom sins are forgiven and sinners justified. When many Jews reject the message, Paul and Barnabas turn openly to the Gentiles, and the word spreads through the whole region.
section.thesis: The Holy Spirit sends the church into the world, and through Paul's proclamation the crucified and risen Jesus is announced as the promised Savior in whom there is forgiveness and a justification the law could never give, a message that divides Israel and opens wide to the Gentiles.
section.frameNote: Four movements: the commissioning at Antioch; Cyprus and the blinding of Elymas; Paul's synagogue sermon in Pisidian Antioch, from the exodus to the resurrection to the call to believe; and the Gentiles' joy set against rising opposition.

units.label: Set apart by the Spirit at Antioch
units.note: the church sends its best into mission

verses.text: Now in the church at Antioch there were prophets and teachers: Barnabas, Simeon called Niger, Lucius of Cyrene, Manaen (who had been brought up with Herod the tetrarch), and Saul.
While they were worshiping the Lord and fasting, the Holy Spirit said, “{{aphorizo|Set apart}} for Me Barnabas and Saul for the work to which I have called them.”
And after they had fasted and prayed, they laid their hands on them and sent them off.

units.label: On Cyprus: Elymas silenced, a proconsul believes
units.note: the gospel confronts sorcery and wins

verses.text: So Barnabas and Saul, sent forth by the Holy Spirit, went down to Seleucia and sailed from there to Cyprus.
When they arrived at Salamis, they proclaimed the word of God in the Jewish synagogues. And John was with them as their helper.
They traveled through the whole island as far as Paphos, where they found a Jewish sorcerer and false prophet named Bar-Jesus,
an attendant of the proconsul, Sergius Paulus. The proconsul, a man of intelligence, summoned Barnabas and Saul because he wanted to hear the word of God.
But Elymas the sorcerer (for that is what his name means) opposed them and tried to turn the proconsul from the faith.
Then Saul, who was also called Paul, filled with the Holy Spirit, looked directly at Elymas
and said, “O child of the devil and enemy of all righteousness, you are full of all kinds of deceit and trickery! Will you never stop perverting the straight ways of the Lord?

Now look, the hand of the Lord is against you, and for a time you will be blind and unable to see the light of the sun.” Immediately mist and darkness came over him, and he groped about, seeking someone to lead him by the hand.
When the proconsul saw what had happened, he believed, for he was astonished at the teaching about the Lord.

units.label: The sermon: Israel's story leads to Jesus
units.note: from the exodus to David to the promised Savior

verses.text: After setting sail from Paphos, Paul and his companions came to Perga in Pamphylia, where John left them to return to Jerusalem.
And from Perga, they traveled inland to Pisidian Antioch, where they entered the synagogue on the Sabbath and sat down.
After the reading from the Law and the Prophets, the synagogue leaders sent word to them: “Brothers, if you have a word of encouragement for the people, please speak.”
Paul stood up, motioned with his hand, and began to speak: “Men of Israel and you Gentiles who fear God, listen to me!
The God of the people of Israel chose our fathers. He made them into a great people during their stay in Egypt, and with an uplifted arm He led them out of that land.
He endured their conduct for about forty years in the wilderness.
And having vanquished seven nations in Canaan, He gave their land to His people as an inheritance.
All this took about 450 years. After this, God gave them judges until the time of Samuel the prophet.
Then the people asked for a king, and God gave them Saul son of Kish, from the tribe of Benjamin, who ruled forty years.
After removing Saul, He raised up David as their king and testified about him: ‘I have found David son of Jesse a man after My own heart; he will carry out My will in its entirety.’
From the descendants of this man, God has brought to Israel the Savior Jesus, as He promised.

units.label: The resurrection and the offer of forgiveness
units.note: raised, never to see decay; justified through Him

verses.text: Before the arrival of Jesus, John preached a baptism of repentance to all the people of Israel.
As John was completing his course, he said, ‘Who do you suppose I am? I am not that One. But there is One coming after me whose sandals I am not worthy to untie.’
Brothers, children of Abraham, and you Gentiles who fear God, it is to us that this message of salvation has been sent.
The people of Jerusalem and their rulers did not recognize Jesus, yet in condemning Him they fulfilled the words of the prophets that are read every Sabbath.
And though they found no ground for a death sentence, they asked Pilate to have Him executed.
When they had carried out all that was written about Him, they took Him down from the tree and laid Him in a tomb.
But God raised Him from the dead,
and for many days He was seen by those who had accompanied Him from Galilee to Jerusalem. They are now His witnesses to our people.
And now we proclaim to you the {{euangelizo|good news}}: What God promised our fathers
He has fulfilled for us, their children, by raising up Jesus. As it is written in the second Psalm: ‘You are My Son; today I have become Your Father.’
In fact, God raised Him from the dead, never to see decay. As He has said: ‘I will give you the holy and sure blessings promised to David.’
So also, He says in another Psalm: ‘You will not let Your Holy One see decay.’
For when David had served God’s purpose in his own generation, he fell asleep. His body was buried with his fathers and saw decay.
But the One whom God raised from the dead did not see decay.
Therefore let it be known to you, brothers, that through Jesus the {{aphesis|forgiveness}} of sins is proclaimed to you.
Through Him everyone who believes is {{dikaioo|justified}} from everything from which you could not be justified by the law of Moses.
Watch out, then, that what was spoken by the prophets does not happen to you:
‘Look, you scoffers, wonder and perish! For I am doing a work in your days that you would never believe, even if someone told you.’ ”

units.label: Gentile joy and rising opposition
units.note: a light for the Gentiles, salvation to the ends of the earth

verses.text: As Paul and Barnabas were leaving the synagogue, the people urged them to continue this message on the next Sabbath.
After the synagogue was dismissed, many of the Jews and devout converts to Judaism followed Paul and Barnabas, who spoke to them and urged them to continue in the grace of God.
On the following Sabbath, nearly the whole city gathered to hear the word of the Lord.
But when the Jews saw the crowds, they were filled with jealousy, and they blasphemously contradicted what Paul was saying.

Then Paul and Barnabas answered them boldly: “It was necessary to speak the word of God to you first. But since you reject it and do not consider yourselves worthy of eternal life, we now turn to the Gentiles.
For this is what the Lord has commanded us: ‘I have made you a light for the Gentiles, to bring salvation to the ends of the earth.’ ”
When the Gentiles heard this, they rejoiced and glorified the word of the Lord, and all who were appointed for eternal life believed.
And the word of the Lord spread throughout that region.
The Jews, however, incited the religious women of prominence and the leading men of the city. They stirred up persecution against Paul and Barnabas and drove them out of their district.
So they shook the dust off their feet in protest against them and went to Iconium.
And the disciples were filled with joy and with the Holy Spirit.

aphorizo.gloss: To mark off, set apart, dedicate for a purpose. The Spirit sets apart Barnabas and Saul for the mission. The same root lies behind Paul's description of himself as set apart for the gospel, Romans 1:1; the sending of the church begins with God's own claim.

euangelizo.gloss: To announce good news, to preach the gospel. Paul's whole sermon is this word in action: the promise made to the fathers has been fulfilled in the raising of Jesus. The good news is not advice but the announcement of what God has already done.

aphesis.gloss: Release, pardon, forgiveness; the letting go of a debt. Through Jesus the forgiveness of sins is proclaimed. It is the heart of the offer: not that hearers must earn release, but that release is announced to them in the risen Christ.

dikaioo.gloss: To justify, to declare righteous, to acquit. Everyone who believes is justified from everything the law of Moses could not justify them from. Here in Paul's first sermon is the seed of the doctrine unfolded in Romans and Galatians: a right standing given through faith in Christ, not achieved by law.

basic.context: The church at Antioch, rich with prophets and teachers, is worshiping and fasting when the Holy Spirit sets apart its two strongest leaders, Barnabas and Saul, for a mission. They sail first to Cyprus, where a sorcerer named Elymas tries to keep a Roman official from the faith and is struck blind, and the official believes. Then they reach Pisidian Antioch, where in the synagogue Paul preaches his first recorded sermon, walking through Israel's history to arrive at Jesus, crucified, risen, and offered as the Savior in whom sins are forgiven. Many Jews reject the message, so Paul and Barnabas turn to the Gentiles, who receive it with joy.
basic.hermeneutics: Follow the sermon's shape: God's saving acts in Israel's past all lead to Jesus. Paul preaches the resurrection as the fulfilment of God's promises and then presses the application, that in Christ there is a forgiveness and a justification the law could never provide. Notice the pattern that will repeat through Acts: the gospel goes to the Jew first, provokes division, and opens to the Gentiles, and the word keeps spreading.
basic.originalLanguages: Key words carry the passage. The Spirit says to set apart, aphorizo, Barnabas and Saul. Paul announces the good news, euangelizo, that God kept His promise by raising Jesus. And he presses home two gifts: aphesis, the forgiveness of sins, and dikaioo, to be justified, declared righteous, which everyone who believes receives but the law of Moses could never give.
basic.typology: David is the pattern and the pointer. God found in David a man after His own heart, yet David died and saw decay. Jesus, David's greater son, is raised never to see decay, inheriting the sure mercies promised to David. The exodus God worked with an uplifted arm foreshadows the greater rescue announced in the risen Christ.
basic.christ: Christ is the whole burden of the sermon. The story of Israel narrows to Him: the promised Savior from David's line, crucified as the prophets foretold, raised by God never to see decay, and now proclaimed so that all who believe are forgiven and justified. The resurrection is central, proven from Psalm 2 and Psalm 16, and it is the ground of the offer of salvation.
basic.god: God is the one who acts throughout: He chose the fathers, led Israel out, gave David, kept His promise, and raised Jesus from the dead. The mission itself is God's initiative through the Spirit. And God's saving purpose reaches beyond Israel: He has appointed His servant to be a light for the Gentiles and salvation to the ends of the earth.
basic.crossReferences: Psalm 2:7 and Psalm 16:10 are quoted to prove the resurrection of the Messiah. Isaiah 49:6 supplies the commission to be a light for the Gentiles. Habakkuk 1:5 warns the scoffers who reject the word. Romans 4 and Galatians 2 unfold the justification by faith that Paul first announces here.
basic.oneStory: This is the launch of the mission that carries Acts forward: the ascended Christ, by His Spirit, sends the church out, and the gospel begins its journey from Antioch toward the ends of the earth. Paul's sermon gathers up the whole Old Testament story and shows it flowing to Jesus, and the turning to the Gentiles fulfils the ancient promise that God's salvation would reach every nation.

context.literary:
Acts 13 is a hinge. Up to verse 12 Luke writes of 'Barnabas and Saul'; from verse 13 he writes 'Paul and his companions', and from then on Paul leads. The change of name from Saul to Paul in verse 9, the first time Luke uses it, falls at the very moment Paul faces the sorcerer, and the narrative quietly shifts its centre of gravity. The chapter has three movements: the sending at Antioch, verses 1 to 3; the encounter on Cyprus, verses 4 to 12; and the long episode at Pisidian Antioch, verses 13 to 52, where the sermon sits in the middle with a before and an after.

The sermon is carefully built. It has three parts, each opened by a direct address. Verse 16 begins 'Men of Israel and you Gentiles who fear God' and covers Israel's history up to the coming of Jesus through John the Baptist, verses 16 to 25. Verse 26 begins 'Brothers, children of Abraham, and you Gentiles who fear God' and tells of the death and resurrection of Jesus, with its proof from the Psalms, verses 26 to 37. Verse 38 begins 'Therefore let it be known to you, brothers' and presses the offer of forgiveness, then ends in a warning from the prophets, verses 38 to 41. History, event, application. The synagogue leaders had asked for a 'word of encouragement', verse 15, and Paul gives one that moves through warning to promise.

Luke also composes the Pisidian Antioch scene on the pattern of Jesus' visit to Nazareth in Luke 4:16 to 30. There a reading in the synagogue, a sermon, initial admiration, then rage and expulsion, with an appeal to God's mercy on Gentiles in between. Here there is a reading from the Law and the Prophets, a sermon, an eager reception, jealousy, a turn to the Gentiles and an expulsion. The disciple's path is the Master's.

The chapter ends with a final contrast: the Jews drive them out, and the disciples are filled with joy and the Holy Spirit, verse 52. The word 'but' of grace falls at the end.
context.historical:
The church at Antioch had a leadership as mixed as its membership. Barnabas was a Cypriot Levite, Simeon called Niger came with a Latin nickname meaning dark, Lucius was from Cyrene on the North African coast, Manaen had been brought up with Herod the tetrarch, that is, Herod Antipas who had beheaded John and mocked Jesus, and Saul was from Tarsus. Luke has chosen to name them, and the list reaches from a palace to a synagogue and from Africa to Asia. These are the men the Spirit names when He says to set apart Barnabas and Saul.

The first journey, which most date around AD 46 to 48, sails from Seleucia, the port of Antioch, to Cyprus, where Barnabas had family ties. Salamis lies on the east of the island and Paphos on the west. Cyprus had been a senatorial province since 22 BC, which is why Luke correctly calls Sergius Paulus a proconsul. He is described as a man of intelligence, and he summoned the missionaries himself, a sign that the news had travelled before them. A Jewish sorcerer in the retinue of a Roman governor was not unusual; many officials kept astrologers and magicians nearby.

Perga in Pamphylia is on the southern coast of Asia Minor, and Pisidian Antioch is some one hundred miles north by road through the Taurus mountains, on a high plateau. It was a Roman colony, settled with veterans under Augustus, and had Roman privileges and a mixed population. Jewish communities in that region went back to the settlement of Jewish families from Babylon in Phrygia and Lydia under Antiochus the Great, as the historian Josephus reports. The synagogue service followed a regular pattern: a reading from the Law, one from the Prophets, and an invitation to those with a word of exhortation. Visiting teachers were often asked to speak, which is why strangers like Paul and Barnabas had an immediate platform.

Gentiles who attended the synagogue, whom Luke calls God-fearers, were attracted to Israel's one God and its moral teaching without committing to circumcision. Many of them heard the sermon, and it is their hunger that fills the next week's crowd, verse 44. The 'religious women of prominence' of verse 50 are probably such sympathisers with civic influence, and the rejection comes from a coalition of the city's elites.
context.canonical:
The sermon is built from Scripture and is meant to be read with its sources open. It begins with the exodus, reaching for the language of the Septuagint, with the people led out 'with an uplifted arm', and recalls the wilderness, the conquest, the judges and Samuel. It combines two texts to describe David, God's 'I have found David My servant', Psalm 89:20, and the rebuke of Saul with 'a man after His own heart', 1 Samuel 13:14, which the BSB footnote on Acts 13:22 points to. It cites Psalm 2:7, Isaiah 55:3 and Psalm 16:10 together as evidence of the resurrection, and ends with Habakkuk 1:5. Luke gives later readers a model of how apostolic preaching reads the Old Testament, as a single story with a single goal.

Psalm 2 appears elsewhere in Acts and the New Testament as a royal psalm fulfilled in Christ: in Acts 4:25 to 26 the church used it to interpret the opposition of rulers, and Hebrews 1:5 uses verse 7 to show Christ's superiority to angels. Psalm 16 was the text of Peter's Pentecost sermon, Acts 2:25 to 31, and Paul here supplies the same argument in compressed form. Isaiah 49:6 is the commission first applied to the Servant, then to Christ by Simeon, Luke 2:32, and by Paul in Acts 26:23, and now to the apostles in verse 47. The repeated use shows how the New Testament treats the Servant's mission as shared.

The sermon also anticipates the great doctrines that Paul will write about. The statement that everyone who believes is justified from all that the law could not justify, verse 39, is the first clear statement of justification by faith in Acts, and Romans 3:21 to 24 and Galatians 2:16 will unfold it. The turning to the Gentiles in verses 46 to 48 begins a pattern that Paul repeats in Acts 18:6 and Acts 28:28, and that he explains theologically in Romans 11:11, where Israel's stumbling brings salvation to the Gentiles to make Israel jealous.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Luke gives his readers a model of the apostolic message and a model of how the mission works. The model sermon shows that the gospel is not a new religion discarding Israel's story but the end to which that story was always pointing. Every step of the history Paul recalls, the election of the fathers, the deliverance, the land, the kings, David, leads to a Savior whom God 'brought to Israel as He promised'. The apostles' hearers did not need to abandon Scripture to follow Jesus. They needed to read it to the end.

The model of mission shows that the Spirit leads, the church sends, and the word goes first to Jews and then to Gentiles, not because Jews are favoured but because the promises were made to them. Paul says it was necessary to speak to them first, verse 46, and the order is a matter of the story, not of rank. When the message is rejected, it is not defeated. It overflows. Luke wants those who hear of Jewish rejection and Gentile reception to understand that this was foretold, that it is not a failure of the apostles or a change of God's mind, and that the gospel has always been about the blessing of all peoples.

He also wants Gentile readers to know that they are welcome without being second class. They are addressed in the sermon as God-fearers, they come in crowds, and they glorify the word of the Lord, verse 48.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The narrative reports the sending, the miracle on Cyprus, the sermon and the aftermath. It does not command the church to blind opponents, to shake the dust from its feet, or to lay hands on missionaries in precisely this way. Paul's words to Elymas come from the Spirit in a particular confrontation, and Luke reports them as an event, not as a model for how to speak to unbelievers. The dust shaken from the feet follows Jesus' instruction to His disciples, Luke 9:5 and 10:11, and Luke gives it as an action of protest, not a ritual.

What the passage does teach, by commendation, is the pattern: leaders who worship and fast before they decide, a church that prays and lays hands on those it sends, missionaries who go to those who are ready to listen, and preaching that is built on Scripture and centres on the resurrection. The call to continue in the grace of God, verse 43, is directly applicable. The warning from Habakkuk is a general principle: those who scoff at God's work in their day do so at their peril.

Be careful with the line 'appointed for eternal life'. It is a descriptive statement about what happened to those who believed, and it is a real theological claim, but it is not a command to sort people into the appointed and the not appointed. The church is told to proclaim, not to guess.

debates.question: What does justified from everything the law could not justify, verse 39, mean for the place of the law?

views.label: The law never justified; Christ alone justifies
views.case: The strongest reading is that the law of Moses could deal with certain matters but could never give a righteous standing before God; only through faith in the risen Christ is a person justified from all things. This anticipates Paul's argument in Romans and Galatians that righteousness comes by faith, not by works of law.

views.label: Christ completes what the law began
views.case: Others stress continuity, that the law pointed forward and its sacrifices anticipated Christ, so that justification in Christ fulfils rather than merely replaces the law. Rightly held this honours the law's God-given role as a signpost, though it must not blunt Paul's point that the law could not justify at all.

debates.bearing: Held well, the verse guards the good news that a full and free acquittal is found only in Christ, received by faith, while still honouring the law as God's true word that pointed to Him.

debates.question: What does 'all who were appointed for eternal life believed,' verse 48, teach about God's choice?

views.label: God's sovereign appointment of those who believe
views.case: The verb is a form of the Greek word for to appoint or arrange, in the passive, and the natural sense is that God had ordained these Gentiles to eternal life. Luke has just said that the Gentiles 'rejoiced and glorified the word of the Lord'. Their faith is the visible result of an unseen appointing, as in Ephesians 1:4 to 5, which speaks of being chosen before the foundation of the world. This has long been the reading of the Augustinian and Reformed traditions.

views.label: Those who set themselves in order toward life
views.case: Others take the verb as a middle, so that those who 'disposed' themselves toward eternal life believed, in contrast to the Jews who in verse 46 judged themselves unworthy of it. The contrast between those who judge themselves unworthy and those who place themselves among the saved fits a human response.

views.label: Both together
views.case: A further view holds that the passage joins human responsibility and divine initiative without resolving how. The Jews are charged with rejecting it, verse 46, and the Gentiles are credited with receiving it, verse 48, while Luke elsewhere says the Lord added to the church those who were being saved, Acts 2:47.

debates.bearing: The text is not a puzzle to be solved by the reader. It is a comfort to the Gentile believers that their faith was not an accident, and it must be held alongside Paul's plain statement that those who reject the word are accountable for it.

debates.question: Does Paul's use of Psalm 2:7 in verse 33 refer to the resurrection or to something earlier?

views.label: The resurrection
views.case: Paul says God fulfilled the promise 'by raising up Jesus', and then adds 'in fact, God raised Him from the dead' in verse 34. Romans 1:4 says Jesus was declared Son of God with power 'by His resurrection from the dead', so Paul can treat the resurrection as the public installing of the Son.

views.label: The coming of Jesus onto the stage of history
views.case: A few read the verb 'raising up' in verse 33 as the same one that speaks of God raising up a prophet or a king, as in Acts 3:22, so that the verse speaks of God bringing Jesus into His office, while verse 34 turns to the resurrection. This keeps Luke's care to separate the two clauses.

debates.bearing: Both readings affirm that Jesus is God's Son and David's heir, and the resurrection stands at the centre of Paul's proof, so the difference is one of grammar more than doctrine.

study.originalLanguages:
The Spirit's word in verse 2 uses a perfect tense: Barnabas and Saul are those 'to whom I have called them', a settled call that was in place before the church recognised it. The verb for 'worshiping' in the same verse is leitourgeo, a word with a service background that is used in the Greek Old Testament for the priests' ministry. The believers are serving the Lord, and Paul will later use the same word group when he describes the Gentiles' duty to minister to Jerusalem in material things, Romans 15:27. Worship and mission are one service.

The synagogue leaders ask for a 'word of encouragement', logos parakleseos, in verse 15. This is the same noun that makes up the nickname of Barnabas, huios parakleseos, in Acts 4:36. The sermon that follows is Luke's example of what encouragement means: not comfort for its own sake, but the good news that makes people able to stand. Hebrews 13:22 uses the same phrase for a whole letter.

In verse 18 the Greek manuscripts divide between two spellings that differ by one letter. One means 'He put up with their ways' and the other 'He carried them as a nurse carries a child'. The BSB reads 'endured their conduct', following the first. The second would echo Deuteronomy 1:31, where the LORD carried Israel as a man carries his son. Both fit Paul's survey of the wilderness, and the translators' note does not decide between them. The point stands either way: God was patient with a people who did not deserve it.

The word for the tree in verse 29, xylon, is the same that Peter used in Acts 5:30, 'hanging Him on a tree'. It recalls Deuteronomy 21:22 to 23, where the body of an executed man is to be taken down before night. Luke's statement that they took Him down and laid Him in a tomb matches the law, and Paul will connect the hanging to the curse in Galatians 3:13.

In verses 34 and 35 Paul joins two texts by a shared word. 'I will give you the holy and sure blessings promised to David' is from Isaiah 55:3, in the Greek translation, where the word for holy is hosia. Then Paul turns to Psalm 16:10 and quotes 'Your Holy One', hosion. The common root links them, a technique Jewish teachers used. The blessings promised to David are fulfilled in the Holy One who did not see decay. The word for decay, diaphthora, is the same word Peter used in Acts 2:27.

Finally, in verse 41 Paul quotes Habakkuk 1:5 in a form that follows the Greek translation. The BSB of Habakkuk reads 'Look at the nations', but the Greek has 'you scoffers' or despisers, which is how Paul quotes it. Paul applies the prophet's warning to his hearers: a work is being done in their days that they would not believe even if someone told them.

In verse 52 the verb 'were filled' is in a tense that means a continuing state: the disciples 'kept being filled' with joy and the Holy Spirit. They have been driven out, and the joy does not depend on being welcome.

typology.type: The one hanged on a tree, Deuteronomy 21:22-23
typology.fulfillment: The law said that anyone who is hung on a tree is under God's curse, and the body must be taken down before night. Paul's phrase 'they took Him down from the tree' in verse 29 is chosen with this in mind, as Peter had said in Acts 5:30. The correspondence is exact in form and astonishing in meaning, for the Son of God came under the curse the law pronounced. Paul explains it fully in Galatians 3:13: 'Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us.' The type falls short only in the sense that in the law the curse marked a criminal's shame, and in Christ it marks a substitute's sacrifice, so that the curse ends instead of being left on the tree.

typology.type: The Servant who is a light to the nations, Isaiah 49:6
typology.fulfillment: Isaiah's Servant was told that restoring Israel was too small a task, and that He would also be 'a light for the nations, to bring My salvation to the ends of the earth.' Simeon holds the infant and calls Him 'a light for revelation to the Gentiles', Luke 2:32, and Paul tells Agrippa that the risen Christ would proclaim light to both peoples, Acts 26:23. In Acts 13:47 the apostles say the Lord has commanded this of them. The correspondence is a pattern of mission carried from the Servant to His body. The type is not exhausted in the apostles, for the light is Christ's own, and they shine with a borrowed light, as the one who calls Himself the light of the world sends them.

typology.type: The sure blessings of David and the throne without end
typology.fulfillment: God promised David a descendant whose kingdom and throne would be established for ever, 2 Samuel 7:12 to 13, and promised in Isaiah 55:3 an everlasting covenant of loving devotion toward David. Paul's sermon claims that Jesus is that descendant, since David died and saw decay while Jesus did not. The escalation is from a king who served his generation to a King who lives for ever. Romans 1:3 to 4 states the same pair: descended from David by flesh, declared Son of God by resurrection. The type falls short in that the Davidic line had its failures, and Saul's tragic fate in this very sermon shows how kings may fall. Only the risen Son can hold a throne that has no end.

typology.type: Elymas's blindness, a sign of a larger hardening
typology.fulfillment: The sorcerer is struck blind 'for a time', verse 11, and Paul had himself been without sight for three days when the Lord met him, Acts 9:8 to 9. The echo is deliberate, and the lesson is that the one who was stopped on the road is the one who can say what the Lord does. Many see in it a small picture of the partial hardening that Paul says has come to Israel until the full number of the Gentiles comes in, Romans 11:25. The correspondence is only an illustration, and Luke does not state it, so it should be held lightly. It falls short because Elymas's blindness is individual and temporary, while Romans speaks of a hardening that is in part and that ends in mercy.

study.christ:
The sermon is an argument that the Old Testament is a road with Jesus at its end, and its steps can be traced. It starts with the exodus and the choosing of the fathers, and then the kingship. The Lord promised David that his throne would endure, 2 Samuel 7:12 to 13, and Paul announces that from David's descendants God has brought Israel a Savior, Jesus, 'as He promised'. The word Savior is a title God holds in the Old Testament, and Luke's gospel gave it to Jesus at His birth, Luke 2:11.

It leads to Christ through John the Baptist, who in the sermon is the last of the old order and the herald of the new, humbly saying that he is not worthy to untie the sandals of the one who is coming. It leads to Christ through the passion, in which the rulers 'did not recognize' Him and yet fulfilled the very prophecies they heard every Sabbath, verse 27. Paul's point is that ignorance did not cancel the plan. Peter had said the same in Acts 3:17 to 18.

The resurrection is the centre, and Paul supports it from three texts. Psalm 2:7 shows that God's Son is to be installed by God; Isaiah 55:3 shows that the sure blessings promised to David will come to His people; and Psalm 16:10 shows that God's Holy One will not see decay. David died and was buried and his body decayed, verse 36, but Christ did not, verse 37. The argument is not merely that Jesus rose, but that His rising makes true everything God had promised.

It leads to Christ in the gift. Through Him forgiveness is proclaimed, and through Him everyone who believes is justified. The word through is repeated in verses 38 and 39, and shows the whole offer to lie in Him. What Moses could not give, Christ gives. This anticipates Paul's later statement that the righteousness of God has been revealed apart from the law, though attested by the Law and the Prophets, Romans 3:21.

It leads to Christ in the commission. When Paul and Barnabas say 'I have made you a light for the Gentiles', they use words first spoken of the Servant, Isaiah 49:6. Jesus is the light first, as Simeon saw, Luke 2:32, and He said that it was written that the Christ would suffer and rise, and that repentance and forgiveness would be preached in His name to all nations, Luke 24:46 to 47. The mission is His, and Paul is His instrument, as the Lord told Ananias, Acts 9:15.

A caution: not every detail is a Christ figure. Elymas is not Satan in disguise, and the proconsul is not a type of the nations. The links above are those Paul himself makes in the sermon and those the New Testament confirms.
study.god:
God is the subject of nearly every verb in the sermon. He chose the fathers, made them great, led them out, bore with them, destroyed seven nations, gave the land, gave judges, gave a king, removed Saul, raised up David, brought a Savior, raised Jesus. The listener who tallies the verbs sees that Israel's history is not a human achievement story but God's story, and that the gospel is in continuity with it.

He is a God who speaks to His church. 'The Holy Spirit said' in verse 2 shows that the Spirit is personal, who speaks, who calls, and who sends, verse 4. The mission is not the result of a committee's strategy session but of worship and fasting, in which the church hears a word. That does not mean the church is passive, since leaders lay hands on them and send them off. It means the initiative is God's and the church's task is to be listening.

He is patient. Whether verse 18 speaks of God enduring Israel's conduct or carrying them like a child, either image shows a God who stays with a people who test Him. The forty years of the wilderness are not skipped in the sermon. Paul admits Israel's failures and does not pretend the history was unbroken success. Yet the grace that held them is the grace now offered in Christ.

He is a God who judges as well as saves. The hand of the Lord is against Elymas for a time, and the sermon closes with a warning that those who scoff will perish. This is the other side of the same God who in 11:21 had His hand with the preachers. Grace is not sentimental, and the same sovereignty that raises Jesus judges those who work against His word. The mercy in 'for a time' is a clear sign, though, that His judgment on Elymas is also an invitation.

He is a God of the nations. Isaiah's promise is not reinterpreted but fulfilled: the Gentiles rejoice and glorify the word of the Lord, verse 48. The purpose to bless all families, Genesis 12:3, is not an afterthought. And those who receive the word are 'appointed for eternal life', which means that God's initiative is behind even their believing, as Paul will write in Ephesians 1:4.

He is also a God who keeps His word. Paul's gospel is that 'what God promised our fathers He has fulfilled for us, their children', verses 32 to 33. If the God of the promise is trustworthy, the believer's confidence rests on His faithfulness and not on the believer's grip.

For worship, the passage teaches us to begin with God's acts. The sermon does not start with the listener's need but with what God has done, and the right response is joy. The disciples, driven out of the city, are filled with joy and the Holy Spirit, verse 52, because the God who acts has not stopped.

crossReferences.note: Jesus at Nazareth reads in the synagogue, preaches, is first welcomed and then driven out, after pointing to God's mercy toward Gentiles. Luke shapes the Pisidian Antioch scene to match, so the apostles' path follows the Master's.

The Father's declaration to the royal Son. Paul applies it to the resurrection, saying God fulfilled His promise by raising Jesus. Hebrews 1:5 uses the same verse to show that the Son is greater than angels.

God promises an everlasting covenant of loving devotion to David. Paul reads it in the Greek form 'the holy and sure blessings', and ties it to the resurrection: the blessings promised to David reach his people only through a Son who lives for ever.

David says God will not let His Holy One see decay. Peter used it in Acts 2:27 and Paul uses it here, because David died and his body decayed, so the verse must speak of one greater than David, who rose without corruption.

Anyone hung on a tree is under God's curse. Paul's phrase about taking Jesus down from the tree echoes that law. Galatians 3:13 draws out the meaning for believers: Christ redeemed us by becoming a curse for us.

The Servant is told that restoring Israel is too small a task and that He will be a light to the nations. Paul and Barnabas take up the words as their own commission, because the Servant's mission now continues through those who belong to Him.

God announces a work so astonishing that people would not believe it if told. Paul warns his hearers that the great work is the resurrection and its offer of forgiveness, and that scoffing at it brings the judgment the prophet described.
God promised David a descendant whose kingdom and throne would be established for ever. Paul's whole historical survey leads up to that descendant, whom God has brought to Israel as He promised.

Paul's later teaching on righteousness apart from the law, attested by the Law and the Prophets, received through faith. It is the fuller statement of the offer made in Acts 13:38 to 39, that everyone who believes is justified.

Israel's stumbling brings salvation to the Gentiles to make Israel jealous. This is the theological explanation of the jealousy of Acts 13:45 and the turn in verse 46, showing that the turn is a stage in God's plan and not its end.

The Lord told Ananias that Saul was His chosen instrument to carry His name before the Gentiles, kings and Israel. Acts 13 is the first full unfolding of that commission, with a Roman proconsul, a synagogue and a Gentile crowd.
At the end of Acts Paul again turns from a divided Jewish audience to the Gentiles, quoting Isaiah. The scene at Pisidian Antioch is the first in a pattern that frames the whole book.
John Mark's departure in Perga, mentioned only briefly in 13:13, becomes the cause of a sharp disagreement between Paul and Barnabas. Luke hints at a cost to the mission that he later describes.

study.oneStory:
The story begins with a promise to Abraham that in him all the families of the earth would be blessed, Genesis 12:3. Paul's sermon is a single sweep through the history that carried that promise: the fathers, Egypt, the wilderness, the land, the judges, the king, David. He does not retell it for its own sake. He wants his hearers to see that the whole movement was heading for one Person, so that the line 'children of Abraham', verse 26, is the doorway into the news that God has fulfilled what He promised.

The chapter answers a question that the Old Testament left open. How would the blessing reach the nations? The prophets had foretold a servant who would be a light to the Gentiles, Isaiah 42:6 and 49:6, and a house of prayer for all peoples. In Acts 13 that promise is no longer a distant hope but an event in a Roman colony in Asia Minor. A crowd of Gentiles gather to hear the word of the Lord, they rejoice, and the word spreads throughout the region. The commission of the Servant is now carried out by those who belong to the Servant.

It also continues a pattern of reversals. Israel was meant to be a light, and when Israel's leaders reject the message, it moves outward. Moses had said God would make Israel jealous by those who are not a people, Deuteronomy 32:21, and Paul applies it in Romans 10:19. The turn to the Gentiles is therefore not a retreat from God's promises to Israel but a step in the plan by which, as Paul says, the stumbling brings salvation to the Gentiles and then to Israel again, Romans 11:11 and 25 to 26.

The chapter sets up the rest of Acts. From here the missionaries go to Iconium, Lystra and Derbe, and the question of what Gentiles must do to belong becomes pressing, leading to the council of Acts 15. The justification by faith that Paul announces in verse 39 will become the central theme of Romans and Galatians.

The end of the story is a people from every nation. In the new creation there is a multitude from every tribe and language standing before the throne, Revelation 7:9. Pisidian Antioch is a small anticipation: Jews, converts and Gentiles together hear one word and rejoice in one Lord. The light for the nations, begun in the Servant and carried by His witnesses, will fill the earth.

quiz.q: How did the first missionary journey begin?

options.text: The Holy Spirit set apart Barnabas and Saul as the church worshiped and fasted.
options.note: Verses 2 to 3 show the Spirit initiating the mission and the church sending them off.

options.text: The church leaders decided it was strategically wise to send out missionaries.
options.note: The church did commission them, but the decisive initiative came from the Holy Spirit, not human strategy alone.

options.text: Paul and Barnabas set off on their own to explore new territory.
options.note: They were sent by the Spirit and the church, not acting on private initiative.

options.text: Rome commissioned them to spread a new religion.
options.note: The sending was by the Holy Spirit through the church, not by any imperial authority.

quiz.q: What is the center of Paul's sermon at Pisidian Antioch?

options.text: That God raised the crucified Jesus from the dead, never to see decay, as the Scriptures promised.
options.note: The resurrection is the heart of the sermon, proven from Psalm 2 and Psalm 16.

options.text: That Jesus is the promised Savior from David's line.
options.note: True and important, but the sermon's climax is the resurrection that vindicates this Savior.

options.text: That Israel had a long and glorious history.
options.note: The history is the runway; it all leads to the risen Jesus, which is the point.

options.text: That the law of Moses is the path to righteousness.
options.note: Paul says the opposite: the law could not justify, but faith in the risen Christ does.

quiz.q: What does Paul say a person receives through faith in Jesus?

options.text: Forgiveness of sins and justification from everything the law could not justify.
options.note: Verses 38 to 39 offer both forgiveness and a righteous standing through Christ by faith.

options.text: Forgiveness of sins, so the guilt of the past is wiped away.
options.note: Forgiveness is real, but Paul also stresses justification, a full acquittal the law could never give.

options.text: A better ability to keep the law of Moses.
options.note: The point is not improved law-keeping but a justification the law could not provide.

options.text: Nothing until they have proven themselves worthy.
options.note: The gift is offered to everyone who believes, not earned by proving worth.

quiz.q: Why did Paul and Barnabas turn to the Gentiles?

options.text: Because many Jews rejected the word, and Scripture commanded a light for the Gentiles.
options.note: Verses 46 to 47 give both the rejection and the Isaiah commission as reasons.

options.text: Because the Jewish leaders grew jealous and contradicted the message.
options.note: The jealousy is part of the rejection, but Paul also grounds the turn in God's command in Isaiah.

options.text: Because Gentiles were easier to convince than Jews.
options.note: Ease was not the reason; it was rejection by many Jews and the scriptural mandate.

options.text: Because God had given up on Israel entirely.
options.note: Paul preached to the Jew first and never says God has cast off Israel; the gospel remained open to them.

quiz.q: How does David function in the sermon?

options.text: As a pointer to Jesus: David served, died, and decayed, but his greater Son was raised never to decay.
options.note: Verses 36 to 37 contrast David's decay with the risen Christ, fulfilling the promise to David.

options.text: As the model king whom God loved and used.
options.note: David was a man after God's heart, but the sermon uses him mainly to point beyond himself to Christ.

options.text: As proof that faithful kings never really die.
options.note: The opposite: David did die and see decay, which is exactly Paul's point.

options.text: As an example unrelated to Jesus.
options.note: David is directly tied to Jesus, the Savior brought from his descendants.

questions: The mission began while the church was worshiping and fasting, listening for the Spirit. How much room does your life and church leave for listening to God before acting?
Paul preached Israel's whole story as leading to Jesus. How does seeing the Old Testament flow toward Christ deepen the way you read your Bible?
Paul offered forgiveness and justification that the law could never give. Where are you still trying to earn a standing with God that Christ offers you freely?
The Gentiles rejoiced and glorified the word while others were filled with jealousy. Why do you think the same message brings joy to some and resentment to others?
Paul and Barnabas were driven out, yet the disciples were filled with joy and the Spirit. What would it look like for your joy to depend on the word's advance rather than on comfort or acceptance?

translationNotes.note: The testimony about David, a man after My own heart, draws on 1 Samuel 13:14 and Psalm 89:20, presenting David as the God-chosen king whose greater Son is Jesus.
The quotation is Psalm 2:7; the BSB footnote notes the literal today I have begotten You. Paul applies the enthronement of the Son to the resurrection of Jesus.
The holy and sure blessings promised to David render Isaiah 55:3; the BSB footnote gives the literal the holy, the trustworthy of David. The sure mercies of David are secured in the risen Christ.
The warning to scoffers is quoted from Habakkuk 1:5, following the Greek Old Testament; the closing quotation mark stands as a separate element in the source text.
